CHAPTER 1 — THE SYSTEM AT A GLANCE
The Ninja Creami XL Deluxe (NC501 series) is not a churner and not a blender. In the Master
Architecture’s terms it is a precision vertical lathe: an 800-watt motor drives a dual-stage paddle down
into a completely frozen solid block at roughly 1,800 RPM, micro-shaving microscopically thin layers off
the frozen cylinder. Conventional ice cream leans on 14–20% butterfat and 15–22% sucrose to stay soft;
a zero-sugar, 80 g-protein block instead freezes like a crystalline polymer — which is why surface
geometry, stabilizer load and freeze discipline are hardware-protection issues, not culinary preferences.
The method is a 7-step pipeline in three phases, executed in strict order. T otal fluid per pint: 600–645 g
(21.2–22.8 oz) in a 24 oz (709 mL) tub, never past the Max Fill line.

CHAPTER 2 — THE PHYSICS & FOOD SCIENCE OF
THE BASE
Hydrophobicity and stabilization
Protein isolates resist water integration. Dry protein or gum dropped straight into liquid forms
hydrophobic “glue pockets” that freeze into icy lumps and load the paddle with dangerous resistance.
Hence the system’s first law: stabilizer is always isolated inside the dry matrix before liquid appears
(Step 1), then streamed into a moving vortex (Step 2). Gum manufacturers prescribe the identical
technique — pre-blend with dry powders to prevent “fish-eye” clumps (Chapter 10, Claim 7).
Volumetric expansion and the centre hump
Egg-white albumin and whey trap micro-air during blending and give the base its overrun — but frozen
under a sealed lid, that expansion drives the centre upward into a frost hump. A convex surface deflects
the descending spindle and loads the drive with lateral shear. The countermeasures are layered: the 15-
minute settle, the lid-off first freeze phase, and masher levelling before any spin. Ninja’s manual forbids
processing a pint frozen unevenly or at an angle; the hump itself is documented in community forensic
practice (Chapter 10, Claim 2).
Freezing-point depression — the allulose engine
Freezing-point depression is colligative: it scales with the number of dissolved particles, not their mass.
Allulose (molecular weight 180.16 g/mol) delivers nearly twice the particle count per gram of sucrose
(342.3 g/mol) — a freezing-point depression factor of 1.9×. The system’s dose of 25–35 g (0.9–1.2 oz)
of crystalline allulose per pint therefore softens the frozen matrix measurably, without the
crystallization-in-storage that hardens erythritol-sweetened pints, and without sugar. Published
references confirm allulose depresses the freezing point and supports scoopability (Chapter 10, Claim
9), with the nuance recorded there.
The hydrocolloid anti-slime law
Xanthan, guar and tara are pseudoplastic, shear-thinning hydrocolloids. In a plain isolate base they
suppress ice crystals cleanly at 1/4 tsp (1.0 g · 1000 mg). But in matrices that already carry whey/casein
blends and modified starches (instant pudding mixes), total hydrocolloid load above roughly 0.25% w/
w cross-links into an elastic, rubbery slime. That threshold is the physical basis of the calibration rule in
Chapter 4: blends and pudding bases are halved to 1/8 tsp (0.5 g · 500 mg).
The taste-audit law
Sub-zero temperatures temporarily anesthetize taste receptors: cold dulls sweetness and flavour. The
warm base must therefore taste noticeably over-sweet at the pre-freeze audit; a base that tastes merely
mild warm will eat flat and unpalatable frozen. This is standard ice-cream doctrine, confirmed in the
literature (Chapter 10, Claim 15).
What the collagen is — and is not
Gelatin is a classic ice-cream stabilizer. Hydrolyzed collagen peptides are not gelatin: per GELITA’s
technical data they cannot form a gel network at any useful concentration. In this system, bone broth

CHAPTER 5 — THE 7-STEP WORKFLOW
Step 1 · Precision dry calibration
Dry bowl on the digital scale — 2000 g (4.4 lb) capacity, 0.1 g (0.004 oz) readability. Weigh the protein
powder (1.5 scoops · ~38–45 g / 1.3–1.6 oz), sweetener (3–4 tbsp · 25–35 g / 0.9–1.2 oz), salt (1 pinch ·
~0.5 g) and any spice enhancers. Measure the gum with the magnetic spoon scraped perfectly flush
with the flat metal levelling bar — 1/4 tsp (1.0 g · 1000 mg) for isolates, 1/8 tsp (0.5 g · 500 mg) for
blends and pudding bases. Dry-whisk thoroughly so gum particles are isolated among dry powder
before any liquid exists.
Step 2 · Thermal emulsion vortex
Dissolve the bone broth (1 scoop · ~10 g) and collagen (1 scoop · ~10 g) into the boiling water (150–
200 mL · 5.1–6.8 fl oz, 70–100 °C / 158–212 °F) until translucent. If the permutation carries almond
butter, it dissolves in this hot phase — heat melts the lipids for a clean micro-emulsion. T emper with the
cold milk (250 mL · 8.5 fl oz) and egg whites (100 g · 3.5 oz). Submerge the KitchenAid immersion
blender, establish a low-speed vortex, and stream the dry matrix in over a continuous 90 seconds.
Pre-freeze taste audit (critical): the warm base must taste noticeably over-sweet (Chapter 2). If it
tastes mild, add 1 tbsp (15 mL · ~8 g) sweetener now. There is no correction after the freeze.
Step 3 · The 15-minute micro-foam settle
Rest the base undisturbed for exactly 15 minutes; whipped micro-air rises and collapses. Pour into a
clean 24 oz (709 mL) tub below the Max Fill line, tap the base firmly on the counter three times to
evacuate deep bubbles, and verify: 600–645 g (21.2–22.8 oz) on the scale.
Step 4 · Stratified lid-off freezing — owner canon
Freeze the tub uncovered for the first 2–4 hours at −18 °C to −20 °C (0 °F to −4 °F): unrestricted
vertical expansion prevents the centre dome from ever forming. Snap the lid on and freeze undisturbed
to a total of 24 hours (16 hours absolute minimum) at the same window. Avoid deep chest freezers
below −25 °C (−13 °F) — cement-brick territory that even Ninja’s manual warns against.
DOCUMENTED DIVERGENCE — OWNER CANON
Ninja’s manual instructs freezing with the lid snapped on for 24 hours. The lid-off first phase is
established community technique (T asty Travelers, Kroll’s Korner) adopted as owner canon in this
system because it prevents the hump at the source. It is labelled wherever it appears (Chapter 10,
Claim 3) and never presented as manufacturer guidance.
Step 5 · Masher levelling & perimeter bath
Solid-block check: the pint must be 100% frozen solid. Any soft centre → back to the freezer for 4
hours.
Perimeter bath: warm tap water over the lower half of the tub’s outer walls for 30–60 seconds —
never past 60 s.
Levelling: press the Deiss stainless masher straight down, firmly, shattering any frost peak into a
perfectly horizontal plane. Never twist — tub walls crack.

Step 6 · Mechanical processing & re-spin tuning
Lock the tub into the outer bowl, selector to Full, program Lite Ice Cream — or Sorbet for pure isolate
bases, whose higher shear duration suits dense isolate matrices. Never standard Ice Cream on these
bases (Chapter 10, Claim 4). After the first spin:
Wall scrape: run a butter knife gently around the inner wall — the paddle leaves a ~1 mm (0.04 in)
frost ring it cannot reach — and fold those crystals into the core. Gentle pressure; the manual
cautions against aggressive metal utensils in the pint.
Dry re-spin first: for hard-scoop gelato density, re-spin with no added liquid; blade friction binds
the mass. This is Ninja’s own NC501 procedure (Claim 5).
Splash re-spin: only if the pint stays powdery — 15–30 mL (1–2 tbsp · 0.5–1.0 fl oz) of cold milk into
the centre cavity, then re-spin, for soft-serve texture. Liquid added prematurely makes soup.
Inclusions: strictly by the three-tier architecture, Chapter 7.
Step 7 · Post-spin refreeze & spindle flush — critical
Leftovers are scraped and pressed 100% flat with a metal spoon before refreezing — a peak refrozen is
a spindle hazard at the next spin, and Ninja’s manual requires the same flattening. Then, immediately:
separate the blade assembly from the lid and flush hot running water directly through the central
spindle aperture. Aerosolized dairy and protein mist migrate into the drive-shaft recess on every spin;
unwashed assemblies grow biofilm and seize their locking springs. This step protects the machine, not
the counter.

CHAPTER 7 — THE THREE-TIER INCLUSION
ARCHITECTURE
Inclusions are classified by how they survive the paddle. The class decides the method — there are no
exceptions.
Tier 1 · Machine borehole — approved
Members: cacao nibs (10 g · 0.35 oz), frozen zero-sugar chocolate chips and mini chips. Protocol:
inclusions must be frozen solid in advance. After the spin, drill a vertical borehole roughly 1 in (2.5 cm)
wide to the bottom of the tub with a knife, pour the inclusions into the cavity — never piled on top —
and run the dedicated Mix-In program. Ninja’s manual sets the same architecture: a 1½-inch hole to
the bottom, chopped mix-ins, ~1/4 cup (60 mL · ~35–40 g) maximum (Chapter 10, Claim 12).
Tier 2 · Manual hand-fold — never machine
Members: sugar-free protein dough bits, crunch nuggets, protein-bar chunks. Protocol:never the
Mix-In program — high-velocity blades pulverize soft inclusions into muddy slime. Drop them into the
spun pint and fold gently with a metal spoon.
Tier 3 · Manual knife-swirl — ribbons
Members: zero-calorie caramel syrup, sugar-free chocolate fudge drizzle. Protocol: carve 3–4 vertical
channels through the processed pint with a butter knife, drizzle the syrup into the channels, and swirl
gently twice for artisan marbling.

Every load-bearing procedure in this system, checked against published references on 21 October 2026.
Primary source: the NC501 Owner’s Guide (SharkNinja). Supporting: hydrocolloid manufacturer
monographs (Cape Crystal, JECFA, GELITA), sweetener technical literature (T ate & Lyle, Ingredion,
Jungbunzlauer), Health Canada and USDA / FoodSafety.gov, and established community references
(T asty Travelers, Basics with Bails, Kroll’s Korner, Maria Lucey RD). The Master Architecture’s internal
audit statuses agree with the external check at every point except emphasis — where they differ, this
register governs the wording.
# Claim in this system Verdict What the references say
1 Freeze ~24 h at −18 °C to
−20 °C (0 °F to −4 °F); temper
an over-cold pint
SUPPORTED Manual: freeze “at least 24 hours”;
freezer “between 9 °F and −7
°F” (−13 °C to −22 °C); chest
freezers not recommended. For
over-cold pints the manual
prescribes a few minutes on the
counter. The 30–60 s warm bath is
community practice (T asty
Travelers, Maria Lucey). Note: −25
°C (−13 °F) is the EU manuals’ limit;
the US book’s floor is −7 °F (−22
°C).
2 The centre hump must be
levelled or it risks the drive
NO OFFICIAL SOURCE The manual never mentions a
hump. It does forbid processing a
pint frozen at an angle or unevenly,
and requires smoothing the surface.
Hump mechanics come from
community forensic practice; the
most careful source (T asty
Travelers) distinguishes an angled
freeze from a bump and notes
bumps concentrate in low-fat/low-
sugar bases — this system’s bases.
3 Freeze lid-off for the first 2–4
hours
OWNER CANON The manual instructs lid-on
freezing. Lid-off is widely taught
community technique for hump
prevention. No Creami-specific food-
safety ruling exists; general
guidance favours covered storage
for quality (freezer burn, odour).
Retained as labelled owner canon —
the single clear official-vs-system
divergence in the book.
4 Lite Ice Cream / Sorbet for
lean bases; never standard Ice
Cream
SUPPORTED Manual: Lite Ice Cream is for recipes
low in sugar or fat or using sugar
substitutes — keto and paleo
named explicitly. Standard Ice
Cream is for “traditionally
indulgent” bases. The manual does

not forbid lean bases on Ice Cream;
community consensus is poor
results, not damage.
5 Dry re-spin first; splash of 15–
30 mL (0.5–1.0 fl oz) only if
still powdery
SUPPORTED The NC501 manual’s re-spin
procedure is dry — no liquid
anywhere in it; re-spin is “often
needed for very cold bases.” Adding
1–2 tbsp (15–30 mL) appears in
generic Ninja troubleshooting and
universal community practice,
sequenced after a dry attempt
(Basics with Bails: add liquid only if
still crumbly after two respins).
6 Scrape the icy wall ring after
spin 1, then re-spin
COMMUNITY Universally taught (Basics with
Bails, Maria Lucey RD, Kroll’s
Korner) because the paddle misses
the edges. The manual’s only
adjacent word is a caution against
aggressive metal utensils in the pint
— a gentle knife or spoon stays
inside it.
7 Gum at 1.0 g (1000 mg) per
~650 g base; halve for blends/
pudding; dry-mix against
clumps; overdose = slime
SUPPORTED Published xanthan range in ice
cream: 0.10–0.30% by weight; this
system runs 0.15–0.23%. Overdose
producing slimy/gummy texture is
documented (Cape Crystal), and the
Master Architecture’s 0.25% w/w
cross-link threshold in starch-
bearing matrices is consistent with
it. Dry pre-blending against “fish-
eyes” is manufacturer guidance,
near-verbatim.
8 Guar / tara interchangeable;
pudding mix justifies the
reduced gum dose
SUPPORTED IN PRINCIPLEGuar: 0.1–0.3% typical in ice cream
(JECFA); tara: 0.1–0.3%, “similar
proportions to guar.” Pudding mix is
itself a stabilizer system; published
base recipes instruct choosing one
stabilizer, not stacking them. No
source publishes a numeric
reduction formula — the 1/8 tsp (0.5
g) figure is owner calibration,
consistent with the principle.
9 Allulose (25–35 g · 0.9–1.2 oz
per pint) keeps the pint softer
SUPPORTED, NUANCED T ate & Lyle: allulose depresses the
freezing point in frozen products;
~70% of sucrose’s sweetness;
browns readily. Ingredion: supports
“smooth scoopability.” The Master’s
1.9× factor is the molecular-weight
ratio. Nuance: erythritol’s raw
depression factor is higher (2.8 in
some tables), but it crystallizes in

storage and hardens pints
(Jungbunzlauer); one industry test
found allulose alone texturally poor,
allulose + erythritol better. GI
discomfort at high doses is
documented.
10 Collagen / bone broth in the
base
REFINED Gelatin is a classic stabilizer;
collagen peptides are not gelatin.
GELITA’s FAQ: hydrolyzed collagen
cannot gel and its function is not
texturizing. This book therefore
classes broth + collagen (1 scoop ·
~10 g each) as protein payload; the
gums stabilize. Agrees with the
Master Architecture’s own REFINED
status.

uncooked, 100 g (3.5 oz) per
pint

products for foods that aren’t
heated. FoodSafety.gov: homemade

egg products. Liquid egg products
are pasteurized by regulation. Keep
refrigerated; respect dates; shell
eggs are not pasteurized unless
labelled.

window is the system’s own

g), in fruit/bakery
permutations

CHAPTER 12 — HARDWARE SAFETY & THE HALL OF
MISTAKES
Critical limits
Thermal window: process pints frozen at −18 °C to −20 °C (0 °F to −4 °F). Below −22 °C (−8 °F),
temper before spinning; below −25 °C (−13 °F) the base is a cement brick.
Fill window: 600–645 g (21.2–22.8 oz), never past Max Fill (Ch. 10, Claim 13).
Surface law: the block’s top must be level before the tub enters the machine.
Program law: Lite Ice Cream or Sorbet only, for every base in this system.
Sanitation law: hot-water spindle flush immediately after every spin — protein mist in the drive
recess becomes biofilm and lock failure.
The Hall of Mistakes — forensic register
# Documented error Root cause Override protocol
01 The Stabilizer Slime
Trap
Gum past 1/8 tsp (0.5 g) on casein
blends or pudding bases cross-links
past the 0.25% w/w threshold.
Enforce the 1/8 tsp ceiling; level with
the flat bar; weigh it.
02 Hidden Sugar / Agave
Trap
Vanilla pastes carried in agave or
glucose syrup quietly break zero-
sugar.
Audit the carrier: glycerin or alcohol
only.
03 Soft Inclusion
Obliteration
Machine Mix-In pulverizes dough
bits and bar chunks to mud.
Tier 2 hand-fold, spoon, post-spin (Ch.
7).
04 The Premature Spin Core under 16 h or not 100% solid:
the shaving profile never engages,
texture collapses to slush.
Solid-block check is mandatory; 24 h
standard.
05 Excessive Thaw BathPast 60 s the perimeter liquefies
while the core stays rock-hard.
30–60 s window; edges must stay
structurally firm.
06 One-Program Bias Standard Ice Cream is calibrated
for soft, fat-rich bases; lean blocks
need the higher-shear programs.
Lite Ice Cream or Sorbet, always
(Claim 4).
07 Unnecessary Liquid
Splash
Milk dumped into a powdery first
spin before friction has had its
chance turns the pint to soup.
Dry re-spin first; splash 15–30 mL (1–2
tbsp) only if still powdery.
08 Direct Powder DumpingGum or protein into cold liquid
forms hydrophobic glue pockets.
Dry-whisk first; stream into the vortex
over 90 seconds.
09 The Centre Hump
Violation
A convex dome deflects the
descending shaft and loads the
drive laterally.
Shatter and level with the Deiss
masher — straight down, never twist.
10 Overflow Freezing Past Max Fill, expansion chokes the
motor and kills overrun.
Weigh the fill: 600–645 g (21.2–22.8
oz), every pint.
